independent.summary: A revoked session keeps a real privilege: `POST /authorize` (and `POST /bridge/authorize`, bridge.js:145) read `req.session.userId` directly with no `requireAuth`/`requireActor`, so the device that was signed out can still call `setMcpUser(userId)` and complete the connector grant — binding the MCP bearer identity to the account and regaining full read/write through `/mcp`. The middleware header claims the check runs on "every request a browser makes", and the docs' carve-out is about *revoking existing* connector tokens (KOL-014), not about a revoked session minting a new grant.

`GET /auth/me` is not behind `requireAuth` and only checks `User.exists`, so a revoked browser is answered `{authenticated:true}` and App.vue shows it a signed-in wiki until the first tenant request 401s — the same "signed in to a wiki that answers 401 to everything" state KOL-038 closed for deleted accounts, now reachable for revoked ones.

grades.reason: `runRevoke` returns early while `revokeSaving` is true and the submit button is `:disabled="revokeSaving || !revokePassword"`, so a double click cannot send a second request; the stated scenario (no way to cancel) also ignores the Cancel button.

The invalidation logic is implemented in the same diff (`sessionOutlivedCredentials` plus the checks in `requireAuth`/`requireActor` in server/src/middleware/auth.js), and the scenario described (account deletion signing other devices out) is not what the spec line claims.
The route is implemented in the same diff at server/src/routes/auth.js:1129 and is covered end-to-end by server/tests/http/sessionRevocation.test.js.

`refuseRevoked` passes a callback to `destroy`, logs the failure and deliberately still answers 401 — documented and correct, since an unauthenticated caller must not be told it is signed in because the store write failed.
The call is inside a `try` whose `catch` logs and answers 500; a deliberately generic message is the codebase's error-shape rule (tests/http/errorShape.test.js), not missing handling.
`passkeyRefusal` catches its own verification errors and returns a reason string, and the whole handler is wrapped in try/catch; nothing is unhandled.
`User.updateOne` is inside the handler's try/catch, and its `matchedCount` miss is handled explicitly with a 401.
`closeStreamsForUser` is synchronous and inside the same try/catch; a generic 500 body is the required error shape, not a defect.
The test does exactly that — `assert.equal(await storedSession(other.sid), null, 'the revoked session must be destroyed, not merely refused')` — using a MemoryStore held by the suite.

These are test-process logs of ephemeral in-memory-mongod ids at a configurable level defaulting off in CI, and the production logs deliberately carry ids rather than emails; no sensitive data is exposed.
The stub is restored in a `finally` block, and `node --test` gives each file its own process, so no other test can see it.

triageGrades.reason: The change is entirely about session authentication — new re-authenticated route, new checks in both auth middlewares, and a new User field.
No secret, key or credential material is added or changed; the new env vars are log-level knobs only.
Nothing touches billing, quotas or AI spend.
The change does destroy state irreversibly — every other session is destroyed in the store by `req.session.destroy` in `refuseRevoked`, and the account timestamp bump cannot be undone.
No outbound calls to any third-party service; WebAuthn verification is a local library.
No version bump, deploy config, migration script or release artifact is touched.

summary: All 11 local findings are false positives — four are generic "no error handling" complaints about calls already inside try/catch, two assert the diff lacks code it plainly contains, and one claims a store assertion the test actually makes — while the two real residual gaps (revoked sessions can still bind the MCP connector identity via `POST /authorize`, and `GET /auth/me` ignores the revocation) were missed.}
